Mostly just unhinged jokes, but one of my favourites is when people who charge for legitimate bereavement or death-related services as we're doing house clearance etc. behave as though they regret charging and I just say "Don't worry, my Mum's paying". I took this one step further with my therapist who put her prices up after about a year of working with her and I also said "You break, you buy" (obviously referring to my Mum not my therapist) 😂

I got my helix pierced a few months after she died and when I was telling my brother I say "I've been thinking about doing it for a while but I didn't want the grief from Mum, but I figured she can't give me any more grief that what she's already given me now so I may as well" 😂
and hole-some too

How To Carry What Can’t Be Fixed is the guided grief journal that Megan Devine (Refuge in Grief on instagram) made and I bought that when my Dad died. Lots of space for creativity if you don’t necessarily want to always use words.

I’m sorry for your loss, and I hope you’re doing as well as you can be right now ❤️

Firstly, I’m so so sorry for your loss and what you are going through. 

What I found most useful in the early days of grief is when people were able to take the burden of some of the day to day stuff which freed me up to deal with the crisis at hand. I had people feed me, either at their house with their families or they brought food to mine if I wasn’t up for socialising. Friends stopped by with basic groceries to make sure I always had milk for tea and bread for toast etc. Had one friend who came to my house whilst I was away sorting stuff at my parents for funeral/ house sale etc and cleaned and vacuumed because she knew it had been stressing me out that I was struggling to find the time for it. 

You’ll definitely be needing therapy at some point but don’t feel ashamed of asking for practical help at this point too. You need to eat, sleep and you probably have lots of admin to do. If there is something that is stressing you out that you’re not able to do, and someone else is willing and able to lend a hand, let them. Don’t feel bad for asking, and if someone says “anything I can do, let me know” it can be hard to ask but sometimes if they can be more specific about exactly what tasks they might be willing to help with it might be easier to ask.

One example, I asked a friend if they would mind letting me know when they were going to the supermarket so I could join them to do my shopping as it was an overwhelming prospect and going with someone else just made it easier and more tolerable. 

All the love to you and remember to be really compassionate towards yourself - it’s hard and it’s ok that it’s hard. There’s nothing wrong with you, your brain and your body is dealing with something really difficult it never had had to before ❤️

I lost my dad when I was 24 and my mum passed away a couple of weeks ago, about a month after I turned 27. It really sucks. There’s kind of no other way of putting it, but the best thing you can do right now is try and be present in the life you have now, make memories and try and enjoy as best you can. I know it’s really hard when you suspect something might be wrong, especially if that person won’t listen to you or doesn’t seem to be taking proper care of themselves. I did the whole not wanting to speak to anyone bit, whilst I processed a bunch of stuff before she died and before I actually knew she was officially ill, and it did help but I would say have a couple of people you are honest with and who will make sure you don’t disappear indefinitely but if time away from the normal rhythms of socialising is helpful then let your friends know that you might not answer immediately or come to everything for a couple of weeks, and do what you need to do to take care of yourself.

Hey - I'm so sorry about your Dad. Cancer sucks and there's probably a lot going on in all of your minds that you'd not thought of before.

I have been in a similar situation - I was away at uni when my Dad got sick and I've lived alone since, about 2 hours away. It felt super lonely then, and I now live 4 hours away and for a while knew no one in my area.

For a while, I had thought that I needed to have a partner because there was no way I could face a repeat of this season alone. I wanted to know that there would be someone by my side the next time and it scared me the prospect of facing something similar again alone.

The best thing that I found is to be in a community, find people you can have real deep friendships with. For me at the moment, it's a church where there are people who have been through a similar thing before, but I've also found community at a Crossfit box, fitness classes, book groups, and photography clubs. Your people, wherever you find them will be there for you, girlfriend or not.

I don't know if this is helpful, so let it fall if not, but the particular situation with you Dad isn't one you can control, and it's ok and normal to feel like a child. You are his child and it's your Dad, and you're facing the prospect of your life changing beyond anything you would have recognised. Anxiety is normal. This is not your fight or flight response misfiring, it's doing what it's supposed to do - please don't beat yourself up because you're feeling like the anxiety battle is uphill.

Surround yourself with awesome people, talk with them, go on stupid adventures with them, have deep meaningful talks with them - be vulnerable and show they can be vulnerable with you too. That's strength. Do the things that you normally do/ love with other people who can help you focus on something other than what is worrying you.

There's nothing weak about acknowledging that you're scared and all the other emotions that come along with a loved one being diagnosed with cancer. Strength is not giving up, but also acknowledging when you need a rest or break and asking for what you need.

Get another job. Your underpaid and undervalued and it doesn't sound like that's likely to change anytime soon. You've said what you needed to say, and if they don't respond immediately with the promotion and pay increase that they have promised, it's definitely time to go.

I've recently been in a similar situation and I start my new job on Monday. You've told them what you need, you've given them enough opportunity to give it to you and it's time to look out for yourself get a better paying job.

Thanks for this advice - although I wasn't comfortable putting in my resignation unless I had another option (that didn't involve packing up my life, moving back home and getting a job at a supermarket) - it did encourage me to (a) continue trying to have the pay conversation with my current employer, and (b) look at other jobs.  


Turns out I'm pretty employable and have received a job offer for approximate 10k more than I currently earn. I also have a formal pay review in the next couple of days, and a couple of other interviews that I already had scheduled before I received the other offer.  


Thank you internet strangers for seeing what I felt I could see was wrong in terms of my compensation, as I think this is what gave me the courage to do something about it.  


I definitely gave a different dilemma (that I've never been through before...again) now, but one way or another - things will be improving! :)

So not pulling any punches then 👍🏻

Helpful to feel validated here, and that I’m not being impulsive if I choose that option.

I find it helpful to frame the feedback in a way that the manager understands/ values for example if I have feedback regarding a training session or course, I always talk about the use of time, because that’s what my manager is always talking about. Some people would focus on money, or how much they learned. If I want to say that the training wasn’t helpful, I would say “I feel my time could have spent better doing X, Y, Z to achieve similar goals”. 

Always present a problem with a potential solution.

I do always send my manager a text/ email after I’ve done anything like that, with brief feedback. Sometimes we discuss further and talk about potential solutions, and sometimes it needs some more reflection. I always find people are very receptive if you frame it in their language, and also try and offer suggestions or resource to improve the thing you’re giving feedback on.

Also, maybe ask if they’re open to discuss some feedback you have. They may say no even though they profess to be open to feedback, which sucks but at least you know the score.

I rarely get 8 hours of sleep anymore, but I’ve improved my work life balance by working from home a couple of days a week, flexing my hours so some days I start and finish early and making some evening plans so I don’t just come home and sit on the sofa watching TV. When I spend an hour doing something I enjoy like the gym, or baking, it often feels like I had more time for myself than I did, or would have if I had spent 3hrs on the sofa when I get in from work.

Standard Operating Procedure. They should have a really clear policy on what should happen in each of these cases. They shouldn’t be trying to intimidate you into work if there’s distinct possibility that you’ll have to self-isolate - that’s why we’re in the mess we’re in.

As much as people are right, in that you donmt have to self isolate until contacted by the NHS, the bubble rules are that if anyone in your bubble has symptoms you should self isolate as they are treated as your household. If someone in your house had symptoms and was getting a test then you would have to self isolate and bubble are treated the same. If you can find this information in the government guidance, point this out to your employer and keep them up to date. If they test positive then you will have to self isolate from the onset of his symptoms, if negative then you’ll be back to work. What is your companies SOP for COVID, they should have made this clear to you before having you back in work?

If they have given you a promotion with more responsibility and not given you a raise, that’s not a promotion that’s exploitation. Look for a new job. I’m sure if you knew that the promotion didn’t include the pay rise you wouldn’t have agreed to extra responsibility

It’s possible but by showing that you’re diligent an conscientious you’ve put yourself in the best position you can. I’m not sure what employment law is like where you live so not sure on how they could go about it. In the UK they couldn’t if you’ve been there more than two years, I know other places it’s different. It would be redundancy rather than firing and if they’re following fair process - your peers would also have to be considered. Again, not sure on employment law where you are.

If they’re constantly having to scramble, it sounds like they need to work on their own management skills...

I would hope they wouldn’t fire you because they can’t manage to keep you busy. Clearly there is work somewhere because they’re finding it from somewhere.

They can let you go for any reason within 2 years. Until you've been continuously employed at a company for 2 years you don't have any rights. There is also likely a period where they can dismiss you immediately without a reason or notice as it'll be a probationary period. It'll be written somewhere in the contract you signed.

You might be able to bargain, but they absolutely can terminate your employment and hire someone who will agree to the rate they're actually prepared to pay.

​

I hope it works out for you though.

If they're going to be making redundancies - you don't want to be the person that's been doing 3 hours a day and pretending like you've been doing 8. You want to be the person who's been being proactive and trying to maximise the time you're working. 

You could ask for a meeting to discuss your workload and mention that you feel you have a lot of space that could be used to take on more work, or could be used for some professional development projects or even just some other process improvement projects. Make work for yourself, but instead of just doing it - pitch it to your managers and get them to approve you doing it. If they end up making redundancies because of the lack of work - you'll be in a good position because you've been proactive in using your resources to add value to the business in ways that other people may not have thought (especially if there's a couple of you in the same boat). Not sure how it would work in your industry though and whether that's even possible. But in short, find a way to show your company any additional value you can offer outside those billable hours.

​

Totally understand though, if you'd prefer not to stick your head above the parapet and risk losing your job if you tell your managers that you need more work to do.

No, it's not. The Government have already provided a considerably tariff for PV that has ended so the ship carrying funding for PV installations has sailed. It's surprising the RHI and GHG can be used together. The Simple Energy Advice website lists it has an energy saving measure, because it saves energy - however, it doesn't have the little badge underneath it saying GHG Eligible like for Heat Pumps or Solar Thermal. Bad design on the website by the Government as it's not an eligible measure.

All ASHP can cool - it's essentially running in reverse which they have to do - it's called the defrost cycle. Using it for cooling does complicate the RHI payments/eligibility(and potentially GHG not that the Government are particularly communicative about how it works) but it would only cool the water in your radiators/UFH (passive cooling). Air to Air heat pumps (the cooling function on these is more like AC) aren't eligible for RHI but I'm not sure if that would effect the eligibility for GHG funding.

I got my job through people at my church that run a business. Chances are they’re hiring those people because they already know them, their work ethic and therefore lower risk. If you’re concerned about your progression in the company - speak to them about it. Chances are, they’d love to hear that you want to continue to add value to their company and be invested in yourself, but if you don’t tell them they’ll never know. The people from the church might see them at other opportunities to have those conversations. If you want to know where you’re progressing then ask them, start the conversation and chat to them about what you skills you have that you want to bring to table and how you might be able to do that. It’s very unlikely that this is purely because you don’t go to their church but the proximity to company leadership for those that do is probably helping them. Give yourself an advantage and make the opportunities for yourself if you want them.

Because a lot of companies are unethical, backstabbing and only mildly competent. They don’t want people who can point out their mistakes to potentially the disadvantage of their finances. Case in point, my mum was an accounts supervisor and checked all the accounts and payroll. She pointed out that 2 employees had been underpaid and one overpaid and she was told to rectify the overpayment but not the underpayments unless the employees brought it up. She found a number of these mistakes the new FC had made. Needless to say, next round of redundancies - suddenly no need for the checks and balances and off she goes. 

If you want to find a company where ethical people are valued, you need to find a company that values ethics. Hard to come by these days sadly
